draft.definition: סְדֹם names the city of Sodom.

analysis.evidence: In מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם, “the king of Sodom,” סְדֹם names the city he rules.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. It completes the construct phrase מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם.

analysis.evidence: וַיֵּצֵא מֶלֶךְ סְדֹם לִקְרָאתוֹ says that the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram. The following אַחֲרֵי שׁוּבוֹ places the meeting after Abram’s return from defeating the kings.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לִ־ introduces the Qal infinitive construct קְרָאת. The third-person masculine singular suffix וֹ is the object of the meeting.

analysis.evidence: אַחַרֵי governs שׁוּבוֹ, “his return.” The phrase אַחַרֵי שׁוּבוֹ places the king of Sodom’s going out to meet Abram after Abram returned from defeating the kings.
analysis.morphology: אַחַרֵי is the longer form of the Hebrew preposition אַחַר. It has no attached prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אַחַרֵי שׁוּבוֹ מֵהַכּוֹת means “after he returned from defeating” Chedorlaomer and the kings with him. The king of Sodom went out to meet Abram on his return.
analysis.morphology: Qal infinitive construct with a third-person masculine singular suffix marking Abram as the subject.
analysis.sense: go back, return from a place or activity

analysis.evidence: אַחֲרֵי שׁוּבוֹ places the action before Abram’s return. The two direct-object markers introduce Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him as the opponents Abram defeated.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition מֵ־ means “from.” הַכּוֹת is the Hiphil infinitive construct of נָכָה.

analysis.evidence: אֶת marks כְּדָר לָעֹמֶר (Chedorlaomer) as the direct object of הַכּוֹת ‘to strike’. The parallel וְאֶת הַמְּלָכִים ‘and the kings’ introduces the second object of the same verb.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew definite direct-object marker with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Genesis 14:1 gives the full name and title כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר מֶלֶךְ עֵילָם. In 14:17 the same name is written across two tokens, כְּדָר לָעֹמֶר. The first אֶת marks the king as the object of מֵהַכּוֹת, and וְאֶת introduces the other kings who were with him.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. כְּדָר is the first written part of the king’s name. The initial כְּ belongs to the name.

draft.evidence: Genesis 14:17 writes כְּדָר לָעֹמֶר in two parts for the king named כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר in Genesis 14:1.

analysis.evidence: In מֵהַכּוֹת אֶת כְּדָר לָעֹמֶר וְאֶת הַמְּלָכִים אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ, the first אֶת introduces Chedorlaomer as the one struck, and the second introduces the kings who were with him. Genesis 14:1 writes the same name as one word and identifies him as king of Elam.
analysis.morphology: The marked token is the second written part of the personal name כְּדָר לָעֹמֶר. Its initial ל belongs to the name.

analysis.evidence: וְאֶת marks הַמְּלָכִים as a second object of מֵהַכּוֹת, “striking down,” alongside Chedorlaomer. The phrase אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ, “who were with him,” identifies which kings Abram defeated.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ precedes a masculine plural absolute noun. The ending ־ִים marks the plural.

analysis.evidence: In הַמְּלָכִים אֲשֶׁר אִתּוֹ, “the kings who were with him,” אֲשֶׁר introduces the clause identifying the kings who accompanied Chedorlaomer.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew relative particle, uninflected, with no prefix or suffix.
